title: Four Reasons Why Jason Wilcox Is to Blame for Man Utd’s Latest Mess
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Andrew Headspeath5:00 PM ESTJason Wilcox has not covered himself in glory at United. /  James Gill/Danehouse/Getty ImagesJason Wilcox has become a favorite for TV broadcaster cutaways in recent months. Manchester United’s increasingly beleaguered sporting director gives great hangdog face and appears to be shrinking further into his overcoat with each defeat.
He was name-checked in Lisandro Martínez’s explosive rant last month, with the defender further putting Wilcox in the spotlight with the sentence “I expect more from our technical director.”

While Michael Carrick has now gone from Old Trafford, Wilcox remains as one of the most public faces of United’s recent shortcomings; TV cameras poised ready to pick him out at the next sign of trouble when domestic soccer resumes following the international break.

In many ways, Wilcox was in the wrong place at the wrong time for United. The former Blackburn Rovers winger joined from Southampton in 2024 as technical director, working under then sporting director Dan Ashworth, as part of the INEOS overhaul of the club’s hierarchy.

Seemingly, it was to be Wilcox’s remit to implement the strategy designed by Ashworth and CEO Omar Berrada. However, after Ashworth lasted just five months in the role, Wilcox was suddenly promoted and found himself in the most important job at the club having only ever spent a year previously in that role (at Championship-level Southampton). He soon found himself in over his head.

Above him, INEOS and Berrada have surely fumbled the big picture, but Wilcox must shoulder some of the blame for United’s historically bad start to the season that has left the club in the relegation zone after 10 Premier League matches.
Here are four ways in which United’s sporting director’s decision making missed the mark.

An appointment doomed from the beginning. / Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesThe appointment of Carrick on a full-time basis felt like a case of (recent) history repeating itself at Old Trafford.
The club legend had overseen an impressive turnaround in form during his half-season interim spell, securing a third-placed Premier League finish and a return to Champions League soccer.
It was essentially a repeat of how Ole Gunnar Solskjær ended up as permanent United boss back in 2019.

While United’s resurrection under Carrick in the back end of the 2025–26 campaign was very good, it was also clearly unsustainable. The players had powered through on momentum, boosted by a lack of European matches and early cup exits.

Carrick, while having done his part as well as he could as caretaker, did not have the experience for the top job and should never have been a serious candidate for an elite club capable of long-term thinking.

After the failures of Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, United needed a clear philosophy and direction. The appointment of Carrick was an admission from Wilcox that he had no idea what his plan was beyond the here and now.

Man Utd have conceded 30 goals in all competitions this season. / Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesUnited’s transfer business of the last two summers has been characterized by an unusual approach: targeting only one position at a time.
In 2025, the Red Devils’ big focus was on forwards, signing Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Benjamin Šesko, as well as goalkeeper Senne Lammens.
This summer, Wilcox and his team went hard on central midfield, with Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos the only players signed for money.
No one would argue that the attack and the midfield didn’t need a makeover, but it was just that the approach neglected the rest of the team.

Several positions were screaming out for strengthening this summer, not least the full back positions, with the aging Luke Shaw’s fitness an ongoing concern and Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui failing to impress.
At center back, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Matthijs de Ligt’s various form and injury issues have left the team further exposed.
